summary: Automatic acceptance of DS parameters from the child DNS operator (RFC 7344, RFC 8078, RFC 9615) means the parental agent, often a registry or registrar, must make decisions about acceptance checks, error and success reporting, and concurrent updates. This Best Current Practice gives recommendations.

eli5.summary: A guide for the office that updates the internet's address book on how to handle automatic updates safely and properly.

subtitle: How registries and registrars should handle automatic DS updates so DNSSEC stays working and nobody is surprised.

tldr.problem: Child DNS operators can ask the parent to set or change DS records by publishing CDS and CDNSKEY records, but registries and registrars have made different choices about checks, reporting, locks and concurrent updates.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives recommendations: verify that requests are consistent and keep validation working, lower the DS TTL to 5 to 15 minutes after a change, report outcomes to the right parties, do not suspend automation for update locks alone, and keep a manual channel.
tldr.outcome: Following the same rules across suffixes means more uniform, predictable behavior for domain holders and fewer broken delegations.

facts.label: Reduction should last
facts.value: At least a couple of days

facts.label: Registrant notified after
facts.value: A prolonged problem, e.g. three days

facts.label: Repeat reports
facts.value: No more than twice in a row

today: RFC 10026 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 246) published in July 2026, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It builds on RFC 7344, RFC 8078 and RFC 9615.

sections.title: Why DS Automation Needs Guidance
sections.content:
RFC 7344, RFC 8078 and RFC 9615 let a child zone publish Child DS (CDS) and Child DNSKEY (CDNSKEY) records that say which DNSSEC parameters the delegation should have. The parent then updates its DS records. The RFC calls this DS automation.

The Parental Agent (often a registry or registrar) has to decide many things: which acceptance checks to run, how to handle timing, what to report, how locks interact, and what happens when several parties can change the delegation. In the registrant-registrar-registry (RRR) model both the registrar and the registry can change the delegation, which adds room for differences.

Existing deployments have not all made the same choices. From a domain holder's view, with names under several TLDs, that behavior can be unexpected and confusing. The core issues come from Section 4.4 of the SAC126 report.
sections.eli5: Many town halls handle address changes in their own way, which confuses people who live in several towns. This guide says how to do it the same way everywhere.

sections.title: What Compliance Means
sections.content:
The guidelines aim for more uniform treatment across suffixes, baseline safety, and no disruption of DNS or DNSSEC. At a minimum, compliance requires support for both DNSSEC bootstrapping (RFC 9615) and later updates (RFC 7344, RFC 8078).

Local policy can take precedence in some cases, for example when a registry faces national cryptographic policy requirements. Not following a SHOULD will generally cause ambiguity and interoperability problems, so operators MUST mitigate issues arising from any deviation. Registries may add further checks in line with local policy.
sections.eli5: Everyone should follow the same rules. If a town has a special reason to do something differently, it has to make sure nothing breaks.

sections.title: Acceptance Checks and Safety Measures
sections.content:
Entities doing automated DS maintenance MUST verify two things and cancel the update if either fails. First, the request must be unambiguous: any published CDS and CDNSKEY records must agree with each other, and all authoritative nameservers in the delegation must serve consistent answers (see RFC 9975). Second, the resulting DS record set must allow DNSSEC validation to continue if deployed, meaning the child's DNSKEY RRset has a valid signature from a key referenced by at least one DS record, using digest and algorithm values marked RECOMMENDED or MUST in the IANA registries.

Parent-side entities such as registries SHOULD allow rollback by reducing the DS record set's TTL to between 5 and 15 minutes when new records are published. The previous or default TTL is restored later, but not before the previous DS RRset's TTL has expired. Below 5 minutes risks excessive queries, and above 15 minutes may slow recovery from mistakes. The reduction should last at least a couple of days. Lowering the old DS TTL first gains nothing, because it adds another wait while caches adjust.

Quick discovery of requests matters too. The best way is for the child DNS operator to send a notification as described in RFC 9859. Periodic scanning is a poorer alternative because it adds policy-dependent delays and does not scale well for large zones.

DNS operators MUST publish both CDNSKEY and CDS records unless the parent's preference is known, because there is no protocol to discover it. If both are present, parents reject inconsistencies rather than guess which is newer. CDS records need only be checked for consistency when their digest type is marked MUST in the "Implement for DNSSEC Delegation" column of the IANA digest registry.
sections.eli5: Before changing the address book, the clerk checks that the note makes sense and that the town will still be findable afterwards. If anything looks off, the clerk throws the note out. For a few days the clerk also keeps the old page easy to put back.

sections.title: Reporting and Transparency
sections.content:
Relevant contacts known to the parent-side entity SHOULD be told about certain DS updates and about DS deactivation. Reporting is useful because a registrar may not know the registry made an automatic change, and a child DNS operator may not know that out-of-sync CDS or CDNSKEY records are being ignored.

For errors, the child DNS operator and the domain's technical contact SHOULD be notified first. The registrant SHOULD NOT be notified unless the problem lasts a prolonged time, for example three days. Child DNS operators SHOULD be told using a report query to the agent domain, as described in RFC 9859 and RFC 9567. The same condition should not be reported too often to the same recipient; the RFC suggests no more than twice in a row, then a back-off.

In the RRR model, a registry doing DS automation SHOULD inform the registrar of any DS changes, for example through the EPP Change Poll Extension (RFC 8590). The current DS configuration SHOULD be visible to the registrant in the customer portal, and the update history MAY be. The RFC also says the Parental Agent should keep structured records of each automation decision, including timestamp, triggering records, nameservers consulted, verification results and the outcome.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, tell the person who can fix it first, and only bother the home owner if the problem sticks around. Keep a diary of every decision so you can explain it later.

sections.title: Registration Locks
sections.content:
Two rules cover locks. Automated DS maintenance MUST NOT be suspended based on a registrar update lock alone (such as EPP clientUpdateProhibited). When the registry performs the automation, it MUST NOT be suspended based on a registry update lock alone (such as serverUpdateProhibited).

The reasoning is that a registrar-side lock protects against accidental or malicious changes, such as through the customer portal, but the registrar can remove it without any out-of-band step. It does not stop actions by the registrar or registry themselves. Suspending automation for it adds difficulty and no real security. A registry-side lock blocks the registrar but not the registry, so it only stops registrar-side automation.

With DNSSEC, a registration can no longer be set up once and left alone, because keys and algorithms may change and the DS records must follow. Authenticated CDS and CDNSKEY requests are legitimate maintenance, and they are still subject to the parent's acceptance checks. The RFC notes that at the time of writing some registries (.ch, .cz and .li) already maintain DS records despite an update lock. Initial bootstrapping should be treated the same as rollovers, since some domains are locked by default and unlocking and relocking is a needless burden.
sections.eli5: A lock on the front door keeps out accidents, but the town clerk has a key anyway. So a locked door should not stop the clerk from doing routine, checked updates.

sections.title: Multiple Parties and Suspending Automation
sections.content:
Registries and registrars MUST offer another channel, such as a manual one, for DS maintenance. It is needed for recovery when the child has lost its signing keys, or when a DNS operator does not support or will not cooperate with automation. Verified requests MUST be executed at the next publication opportunity, whichever channel they arrive on.

Removal is handled with care. A CDS/CDNSKEY delete signal (from RFC 8078) MUST NOT suspend automation, so the registrant can bootstrap again later. Any other removal request, such as via EPP or a web form, SHOULD suspend automation until a new DS record set is provisioned, to avoid re-initialization when the registrant meant to turn DNSSEC off. Whenever a non-empty DS set is provisioned, automation SHOULD NOT (or no longer) be suspended. Resuming automation after an SOA serial change is NOT RECOMMENDED, because routine signature refreshes also change the serial.

In the RRR model, a registry MUST NOT automatically initialize DS records when it knows the registrar gives the domain holder no way to disable DNSSEC later. If the registrar says it does DS automation, the registry SHOULD publish the registrar's notification endpoint instead of its own and not automate.

If both registry and registrar scan, no disruption is expected. During a key rollover they could see different versions and cause flapping, but either DS set keeps validation working and the effect fades once the child is consistent. Notifications to one party's endpoint, or an agreement that only one side scans, remove the issue.
sections.eli5: There must always be a plain old way to fix things by hand. And if you ask the town to erase your page on purpose, it should not quietly write it back the next day.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If inconsistencies between CDS and CDNSKEY records were ignored, risks follow. For example, if a nameserver's domain expires and is maliciously re-registered, an attacker might initialize a DS RRset and then redelegate the domain using CSYNC (RFC 7477), taking over the domain. The same total control is possible if the child's SEP key is compromised, since that key can authorize DS updates or removal when published consistently on all nameservers.

Removing the DS RRset, manually or by a delete signal, ends DNSSEC protection. A mail operator enforcing DANE for a domain could then see delivery disruption, so child and parent DNS operators MUST consider such effects before removing DS records. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If the checks are skipped, a trickster could take over a town's address entry. And erasing the safety seal can break things for people who relied on it.
